props.title: One violin for the aisle, a quartet for the ballroom.

rows.text: One violinist, and the smallest strings booking. It plays a ceremony from the prelude to the recessional, an hour under a dinner for twenty, or the one song at a proposal.

Violin and cello. The cello carries the bass line under the melody, so Canon in D sounds the way people remember it and a processional has weight in a big space. It’s the size most often booked for the ceremony and the cocktail hour together.

Two violins and cello, or violin, viola and cello. The harmony parts arrive with the third player, so the pop songs and the film themes fill out, and it holds a cocktail hour on a terrace or a long dinner at a level the table talks across.

Two violins, viola and cello, the size the quartet repertoire was written for. It’s the booking for a church or a ballroom, for a gala’s first hour, and for a reception that wants the full sound under dinner.

props.html: For a ceremony on guitar, the solo guitarist plays it on steel strings and the Spanish guitarist on nylon. The jazz duo can take the cocktail hour after a strings ceremony, and the DJ the dancing, on the same contract.

rows.text: Strings play all four parts of a ceremony, from the prelude while guests find their seats to the recessional. A violinist watches the aisle, so the processional lasts exactly as long as the walk, and in a church in Denver or Colorado Springs, or a ballroom in the mountains, the quartet carries where one instrument would be lost.
The same musicians walk from the ceremony to the terrace and play Coldplay, the Beatles and Taylor Swift arranged for strings, at a level guests talk across, on the same contract as the ceremony.
A string quartet playing as the doors open is the sound of a black-tie evening. It’s the reception act on a gala’s contract, with the dinner act and the dance floor act on the same one.
A duo or a trio under a dinner for twenty to sixty, so the evening has live music in it and the conversation stays the point.
A violinist or a trio at a dinner at home, a fiftieth anniversary at a club or an eightieth birthday, with the song from their own wedding on request.
One violinist for one song, A Thousand Years or the film theme that’s theirs, at a restaurant table or a trailhead.
Ave Maria, Amazing Grace and the hymns the family chooses, on one violin or violin and cello, in a chapel, at a graveside or at a celebration of life.

props.html: The questions every booking shares, from substitutions to volume limits, are on the full question list. The four instruments, and how a trio or a duo compares, are in what is a string quartet.

items.q: What does a string quartet cost for a wedding in Denver?
items.a: A Denver wedding guide puts a classical string duo or trio for a ceremony or cocktail hour at $800 to $2,000, and a full quartet sits above that. That's the market's figure. Signet doesn't publish prices, so send us the date, the venue and the size you're picturing and we'll price that night.

items.q: How much space does a string quartet need?
items.a: A level spot about ten feet across and eight deep, four seats without arms, and shade or cover outdoors. The musicians bring their own stands and music, and indoors nothing is plugged in. One violinist fits in a corner about four feet across.

items.q: Can a string quartet play outdoors?
items.a: Yes, with shade, cover from rain and level ground, because a violin can't sit in direct sun or get wet. Cold matters too, since strings drift and fingers slow down once the temperature drops into the fifties, so for a mountain ceremony we agree a plan for moving under cover with you ahead of time.

items.q: How loud is a string quartet?
items.a: About as loud as a conversation at the next table. Indoors it plays a prelude, a processional and a cocktail hour with nothing plugged in, and the front table keeps talking. Outdoors, or in a hall where the back has to hear the officiant, a small sound system on one standard outlet carries the strings and a microphone, and the musicians set the level to the space.

items.q: Can you play a song that isn't on the list?
items.a: Yes. Custom arrangements are part of the booking, so a song that isn't on the list can be written out for the size you book, one violin or four. Send the title with the date, and a recording of the version you mean if there's more than one.

items.q: Who plays a classical strings booking?
items.a: Working string players from our roster, and we name them to you when the contract is written. You book the size, one violinist to the quartet, and the same players cover the ceremony and the cocktail hour.
